desc: The FY2024 report covers 1 May 2023 through 1 June 2024 and was released on 14 November 2024, the day after the House Oversight hearing at which Luis Elizondo and Tim Gallaudet testified and five days before Kosloski appeared before the Senate. It records 757 reports - 485 in-period and 272 backfilled from 2021-2022 - with 118 resolved in-period and 174 more finalised by publication, all to prosaic objects: balloons, birds, unmanned aerial systems. Twenty-one cases were flagged as warranting continued investigation by intelligence and science and technology partners on the basis of reported anomalous characteristics or behaviours. It contains the explicit denial: to date, AARO has discovered no evidence of extraterrestrial beings, activity, or technology. It documents the secure reporting mechanism launched at aaro.mil in October 2023 for current or former USG employees, service members and contractors claiming direct knowledge of purported USG UAP programmes dating back to 1945, with confidentiality protections. It cites 50 U.S.C. 3373(k). The report's own numbers are the argument against its conclusion: 21 cases with anomalous characteristics and roughly 900 reports parked in an active archive for want of scientific data is not a null result, it is an unfunded one.

claims.text: The report is submitted under a requirement established in 50 U.S.C. 3373(k), which directs the Director of the Office to report to the appropriate congressional committees not later than 180 days after enactment of the FY2023 Intelligence Authorization Act and annually thereafter for four years.

AARO received 757 UAP reports during the period 1 May 2023 - 1 June 2024; 485 occurred in period and 272 occurred in 2021-2022 but were not previously reported. As of 24 October 2024 AARO held 1,652 reports in total.

Of the 757 reports, 392 came from the FAA and consisted of all of the FAA's UAP reports since 2021; 708 occurred in the air domain, 49 in the space domain, and none in the maritime or transmedium domains.

AARO determined 21 cases merit further analysis by its intelligence-community and science-and-technology partners; 444 cases lacked sufficient data to facilitate analysis and were placed in the Active Archive.
The report states verbatim: "During the reporting period, AARO did not receive any UAP reports collected through national GEOINT, SIGINT, or MASINT platforms."

Section IV.G, headed "AARO Possesses No Data to Indicate the Capture or Exploitation of UAP," consists in its entirety of the statement that "AARO is working with mission partners to formalize a process in the event UAP materiel is captured, drawing on current USG capabilities and operating procedures" - an admission that no such process existed as of the cut-off date.
The report states: "It is important to underscore that, to date, AARO has discovered no evidence of extraterrestrial beings, activity, or technology."

AARO asserts it "is authorized by law to receive all UAP related information including any classified national security information involving military intelligence or intelligence related activities at all levels of classification, regardless of any restrictive access controls, special access controls, or compartmented special access programs," and that there is "no restriction on AARO receiving any past or present UAP-related information, regardless of the organizational affiliation of the original classification authority."

Oak Ridge National Laboratory "provided analysis for a material claimed to be from a UAP," and AARO S&T, in coordination with ORNL, wrote a materials-analysis report and posted it on AARO's website, with supplemental data promised.

AARO posted historical documents relating to KONA BLUE, described in the report as "a Prospective and not approved Special Access Program that was brought to AARO's attention by interviewees who claimed that it was a sensitive Department of Homeland Security compartment to cover up the retrieval and exploitation of 'non-human biologics.'"

AARO received 18 reports from the Administrator for Nuclear Security and the Chairman of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission regarding incidents near U.S. nuclear infrastructure, weapons and launch sites, all categorised by those agencies as UAS; two incursions lasted 53 minutes and 1 hour 57 minutes respectively.

On 3 August 2023 D.C. Cook Nuclear Power Plant security recovered a crashed UAS which was given to Berrien County, Michigan local law enforcement, and "AARO has no further information about the crashed UAS." Separately, the BWXT (formerly Babcock and Wilcox Nuclear Energy) Fuel Cycle Facility in Lynchburg, Virginia observed UAS flyovers on six consecutive nights, 10-15 October 2023.

In May 2023 the Joint Staff issued a UAP GENADMIN message directing Combatant Commands and Services to report all UAP incidents, incursions and engagements to Combatant Command Joint Operations Centers, Service Watch Centers, and respective counterintelligence elements no later than 96 hours after the event.

AARO's named science-and-technology partners are Oak Ridge National Laboratory, the Air Force Research Laboratory, the Georgia Tech Research Institute (developer of the GREMLIN sensor architecture, tested March 2024 and slated for a 90-day pattern-of-life collection at a site of national security), MIT Lincoln Laboratory (prototype processing for FAA and National Weather Service radar), and NASA as focal point for academic and open-source analysis.

connections: 50 U.S.C. 3373 and 50 U.S.C. 3373b are the statutory hooks; 3373(k) creates the report and 3373b creates the secure mechanism for current and former USG employees and contractors to report knowledge of purported UAP programs dating back to 1945

AARO was established on 15 July 2022 by Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen Hicks, renaming and expanding the Airborne Object Identification and Management Synchronization Group; Sean Kirkpatrick (first director, July 2022 - December 2023) to Tim Phillips (acting) to Jon Kosloski, previously of NSA, is the leadership chain across the report's drafting
Oak Ridge National Laboratory is the government-side materials-analysis node, directly parallel to the Nolan-Vallee 2022 protocol

KONA BLUE links AARO's disclosure to the AAWSAP/DIA lineage and to the Department of Homeland Security; AARO's own Historical Record Report Vol 1 ties KONA BLUE's supporters to the cancelled DIA program
Georgia Tech Research Institute (GREMLIN), MIT Lincoln Laboratory, AFRL and NASIC are the technical contractor and laboratory set now built around the UAP problem
The report was drafted in coordination with NRO, NGA, NSA, DIA, MSIC, NGIC, NASIC, NCIS, FBI, DoE, NNSA and NRC among others - the same institutional set named across the legacy-program allegations
The May 2023 Joint Staff GENADMIN routes UAP reporting through Service counterintelligence elements, which for the Department of the Air Force means AFOSI

Rep. Mike Gallagher's May 2022 House Intelligence subcommittee hearing, at which the Wilson-Davis memo was entered into the record, is the immediate legislative antecedent of the reporting regime this document satisfies
dossier.denialPosture: Categorical and repeated: no evidence of extraterrestrial beings, activity or technology; no data indicating the capture or exploitation of UAP; no confirmation of foreign adversarial attribution. The denials are consistently framed as statements about what AARO possesses or has discovered rather than about what exists, which preserves deniability if material is held in a compartment AARO has not in fact penetrated.
dossier.narrative:
Read as a compliance document, the FY2024 report is a study in what a statutory reporting requirement can and cannot compel. 50 U.S.C. 3373(k)(1)(B) enumerates roughly fifteen mandatory content items, and the report walks them in order: events in period, events out of period, analysis by intelligence discipline, incidents over restricted airspace, threats, foreign attribution, breakthrough foreign capability, allied consultation, capture-or-exploitation efforts, health effects, nuclear-asset association, NNSA and NRC consultation, designated line organisations, and a summary of authorised reporting. The statute is well drafted. The answers are mostly negative, and the negatives are the interesting part.

The numbers: 757 reports received, of which 485 occurred in the reporting period and 272 occurred in 2021-2022 but were only reported now. Cumulative holdings as of 24 October 2024 were 1,652 reports. Of the 757, 392 - more than half - came from the FAA, and consisted of the entire FAA UAP reporting log since June 2021. By domain: 708 air, 49 space, zero maritime, zero transmedium; and AARO notes that none of the space-domain reports came from space-based sensors, all being pilot or ground-observer accounts of objects estimated above 100 kilometres. AARO resolved 49 cases in-period, recommended 243 more for closure, judged 21 to merit further analysis by intelligence-community and science-and-technology partners, and consigned 444 to an 'Active Archive' for lack of data. By publication, the office reported 118 resolved and a further 174 finalised, all to prosaic objects.

The key sentence for anyone tracking concealment is buried in Section III.B: "During the reporting period, AARO did not receive any UAP reports collected through national GEOINT, SIGINT, or MASINT platforms." Every input was pilot report, post-mission full-motion video, or FAA log. AARO can search IC databases case-by-case, but nothing was tasked. Whatever else the report establishes, it establishes that the collection architecture of the United States was not being used to answer this question during the period covered.

The second key passage is the nuclear-infrastructure section. AARO received eighteen reports from the NNSA Administrator and the NRC Chairman regarding incidents near U.S. nuclear infrastructure, weapons and launch sites, all of which those agencies categorised as unmanned aircraft systems. Two involved incursions of 53 minutes and one hour 57 minutes. On 3 August 2023 security at the D.C. Cook Nuclear Power Plant recovered a crashed UAS and turned it over to Berrien County, Michigan local law enforcement; AARO states flatly that it "has no further information about the crashed UAS." A recovered object over a nuclear facility left the federal system entirely and the office statutorily charged with anomaly resolution never got it back. Separately, the BWXT Fuel Cycle Facility in Lynchburg, Virginia experienced UAS overflights on six consecutive nights, 10-15 October 2023.

The third is the authorities language. AARO asserts it "is authorized by law to receive all UAP related information including any classified national security information involving military intelligence or intelligence related activities at all levels of classification, regardless of any restrictive access controls, special access controls, or compartmented special access programs," with "no restriction on AARO receiving any past or present UAP-related information, regardless of the organizational affiliation of the original classification authority." This is the exact authority whose absence is the subject of the Wilson-Davis memo - a Deputy Director of DIA being told by a contractor committee that his tickets and statutory authority were not sufficient. The FY2024 report asserts the authority exists. It does not report ever having exercised it against a waived or unacknowledged SAP, nor does it report a single instance of an access denial.

The science-and-technology section names the partner set: Oak Ridge National Laboratory for physics-relevant case analysis and the UAP-material analysis; the Air Force Research Laboratory for propulsion, stealth and sensing assessments; the Georgia Tech Research Institute, which built the GREMLIN sensor architecture that demonstrated functionality in a March 2024 test and was slated for a 90-day pattern-of-life collection "at a site of national security"; MIT Lincoln Laboratory, building prototype processing to recover objects currently filtered out of FAA and National Weather Service radar; and NASA as focal point for academic and open-source work. That is a real, funded, technically competent architecture, and its existence should be weighed against the report's own admission that the office cannot resolve most of its caseload.

Finally, the strategic communications section records that AARO posted historical documents relating to KONA BLUE, characterising it as "a Prospective and not approved Special Access Program that was brought to AARO's attention by interviewees who claimed that it was a sensitive Department of Homeland Security compartment to cover up the retrieval and exploitation of 'non-human biologics.'" AARO's framing is dismissive. But the disclosure itself confirms that a UAP-linked prospective SAP was drafted, staffed toward DHS, and documented well enough that its papers could be posted eight months later.
openQuestions: What the 21 cases judged to merit further analysis actually are, and what became of them
Whether AARO has ever exercised its asserted authority to compel access to a waived or unacknowledged special access program, and whether any access was refused
Which material was analysed by ORNL, who supplied it, and what the chain of custody was
Why no national GEOINT, SIGINT or MASINT collection was tasked against UAP during a full reporting year, and who makes that tasking decision
What happened to the UAS recovered at D.C. Cook Nuclear Power Plant on 3 August 2023 after it was handed to county law enforcement
The identity of the 'site of national security' selected for the GREMLIN 90-day pattern-of-life collection
Whether the report's zero maritime and zero transmedium counts reflect absence of events or absence of a reporting channel from the naval and undersea domains
dossier.whatItIs: The Fiscal Year 2024 Consolidated Annual Report on Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena, produced by the Department of Defense All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO) with an information cut-off of 1 June 2024 and released 14 November 2024. It is submitted to Congress under a statutory requirement at 50 U.S.C. 3373(k) and covers UAP reports from 1 May 2023 to 1 June 2024 plus all prior-period reports not previously reported. It was drafted in coordination with more than two dozen named organisations including ODNI, the Service intelligence centres, NRO, NGA, NSA, DIA, FBI, NCIS, DoE, NASA, the NNSA and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.
dossier.whyImplicated: AARO is not a neutral authority here; it is the office the Department created to be the answer to the question, and this report is the instrument by which it discharges its obligation to Congress. What makes it load-bearing is not its denials but the specific admissions embedded in them. Section IV.G is headed "AARO Possesses No Data to Indicate the Capture or Exploitation of UAP" and its entire body is a single sentence stating that AARO is working with mission partners "to formalize a process in the event UAP materiel is captured" - meaning that as of mid-2024 no such process existed anywhere the office could see. Section VI.C confirms that Oak Ridge National Laboratory analysed "a material claimed to be from a UAP." Section VI.D confirms AARO posted historical documents on KONA BLUE, a prospective and unapproved Special Access Program that interviewees described as a DHS compartment to cover up "the retrieval and exploitation of 'non-human biologics.'" And the report concedes that 444 of the 757 reports lacked sufficient data for any analysis and that AARO received zero UAP reporting through national GEOINT, SIGINT or MASINT platforms during the entire period - the national technical means that would find a concealed program were not pointed at the problem at all.
